2.text: number of his cousins. Some people from the Wolverene River accused this

3.text: man of having murdered one of their friends in a drunken brawl two years

4.text: before: so they wanted to punish him for that. They came to the camp of

5.text: the Anui people armed with rifles and knives, but the master of the camp

6.text: declared that he was ready to defend his guest. His people were more

7.text: numerous. An altercation ensued. The offended party wanted at least to

8.text: take the team of the murderer, since it was the only thing there “dear to his

9.text: heart” (liˊnliñqin); but the accused one flatly refused to part with the team.

10.text: “I will rather die,” said he. So, after some quarrelling and mutual threats,

11.text: the assailants saw the necessity of contenting themselves with fawn-skins, which

12.text: the murderer had brought for sale to the Russians. The skins were twenty

13.text: in number, valued at fifteen rubles. A Chukchee single driver cannot carry

14.text: much on his small sledge. Some time afterwards I saw one of the assailants.

15.text: He said, “Well, after all, he had to go back to his family empty-handed.

16.text: The tea and tobacco, the ‘desire of his heart,’ were taken from him with

17.text: these fawn-skins.” From the Chukchee point of view, this reasoning was

18.text: more or less true. The force of the desire is taken into account independently

19.text: of the real value of the object, in peaceful trading; and a Chukchee is ready

20.text: to pay a threefold price for any trifle that may take his fancy, and could not

21.text: be acquired otherwise. The Russian traders are well aware of this disposition

22.text: of the Chukchee, and make full use of it in all commercial transactions. So in

23.text: this case tea and tobacco were really “dear to the heart” of the accused man.

24.text: MINOR CRIMES. — Minor crimes, on the whole, are followed either by

25.text: personal chastisement or by the payment of weregild. The personal chastise-

26.text: ment is usually preceded by a challenge to a wrestling-match, and inflicted

27.text: after the victory in the dance. I mentioned before¹ the tale of the “Lucky

28.text: Suitor,” in which such an incident is described with characteristic details.

29.text: “The hero married a proud girl, who had previously refused all her suitors. One of them,

30.text: who lived in a neighboring camp, met her outside, threw her to the ground, and scratched her

31.text: face with the point of his knife. The lucky suitor came to her camp shortly after the incident,

32.text: vanquished her in a running-match, and was accepted. The next fall the neighbor who had scratched

33.text: the woman’s face invited the people, saying, ‘Let us again have races and running-matches!’ All

34.text: the people assembled, and all took part in a running-match. The newly married one did not take

35.text: off his outer fur shirt. He ran in his usual clothes. Nevertheless he came back first. All the

36.text: others were behind. Then he sprang forward, and said, ‘Well, come on [for a wrestling-match].’

37.text: His face was inflamed with anger. ‘Who wants to try? Hurry up!’ — ‘Who knows?’ answered

38.text: the others. ‘Let this one wrestle with me!’ and he pointed out the neighbor who in the past year

39.text: had scratched his wife’s face. ‘No,’ says the neighbor, looking down. ‘Hurry up!’ said the other.

40.text: He continued to refuse. Then at last the lucky suitor sprang toward him and kicked him in the

41.text: face. The other one fell down and swooned. After a while he sat up on the ground. ‘Hurry up!’

42.text: He rose, but continued to refuse. Then the lucky suitor caught him, threw him down, and pressed

43.text: him with his knee to the ground. Then he took out his girdle-knife, and cut his nostrils all over,
